content: Adenoiditis refers to the inflammation of the adenoid tissue, which is a lymphoid structure forming part of the Waldeyer ring. This condition is most commonly caused by viral infections, although certain bacterial pathogens, such as Haemophilus influenzae, group A β-hemolytic streptococcus, and Staphylococcus aureus, can also be responsible. If left untreated, adenoids can lead to recurrent sinusitis, chronic or recurrent otitis media, and eventually chronic adenoiditis. Management of adenoiditis may involve medications, such as antibiotics or steroids, or surgical intervention, depending on the underlying cause. Historically, adenoids were once thought to be part of the tonsils and were associated with symptoms of nasal congestion and obstruction. For over 2000 years, adenoidectomy was performed as part of adenotonsillectomy. In the early 19th century, adenoid and tonsil tissues were considered remnants of an unknown infectious disease, leading to their removal. Wilhelm Meyer of Copenhagen was the first to describe adenoiditis caused by adenoid vegetations, which were linked to nasal symptoms and hearing impairment. He is also credited with performing the first separate adenoidectomy. Adenoiditis can be classified into three types: acute adenoiditis, recurrent acute adenoiditis, and chronic or persistent adenoiditis. The adenoids play a role in producing secretory IgA, which provides local immune protection. Studies suggest that IgA levels decrease following adenoidectomy. Adenoid tissue also harbors bacteria from the normal oral flora, such as alpha-hemolytic streptococci, enterococci, Corynebacterium species, coagulase-negative staphylococci, Neisseria species, Haemophilus species, Micrococcus species, and Stomatococcus species. However, adenoids can also harbor pathogenic bacteria, which may lead to infections of the ears, nose, and sinuses. If untreated, adenoiditis can progress to a chronic condition. Acute adenoiditis is primarily caused by viral infections, but bacterial infections play a more significant role in recurrent and chronic cases. Important viral causes include Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The most common bacterial causes are Haemophilus influenzae, group A β-hemolytic streptococcus, and Staphylococcus aureus. Diagnosing adenoiditis can be challenging because many upper respiratory tract infections present similarly. Differential diagnoses include tonsillitis, viral upper respiratory tract infections, sinusitis, and pharyngitis. The prevalence of adenoiditis is not well-documented, but research suggests that bacterial adenotonsillitis accounts for 15-30% of sore throats in children and 5-10% in adults. The condition becomes less common with age, as adenoid tissue undergoes atrophy after the age of 10 and is rarely seen after 15 years. The most significant risk factor for adenoiditis is being a young child. Other risk factors include immunodeficiencies, living in urban environments with increased exposure to pathogens, and the use of immunosuppressant drugs. There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine screening for adenoiditis. Acute adenoiditis typically presents with erythema and edema of the adenoids, which occur rapidly following pathogen infiltration. Symptoms such as fever and sore throat usually develop within 24 hours of infection. Adenoiditis often coexists with tonsillitis due to their close anatomical proximity. Complications of adenoiditis arise from the persistence or spread of the responsible pathogen, usually bacterial. These complications include speech abnormalities, otitis media, acute sinusitis, pneumonia, adenoid hyperplasia, peritonsillar abscess, and sleep apnea. The prognosis for acute adenoiditis is generally good, as it is often a self-limiting condition that resolves within 3-4 days without treatment. There are no specific diagnostic criteria for adenoiditis. However, the presence of inflamed and hypertrophied adenoid tissue observed through flexible or rigid nasopharyngoscopy can support the diagnosis, particularly in cases of chronic adenoiditis. A history of fever, nasal obstruction, and snoring is suggestive of adenoiditis. Common symptoms include purulent nasal discharge, mouth breathing, nasal pain, and sore throat. Physical examination findings may include fever and purulent nasal discharge. Laboratory findings consistent with adenoiditis include neutrophilia, positive throat culture for the causative organism, and positive blood cultures in severe cases. Imaging, such as lateral neck X-rays, may show enlarged adenoids and airway narrowing. Nasopharyngoscopy provides direct visualization of the inflamed adenoid tissue. The primary treatment for adenoiditis is symptomatic management. Medical therapy, including antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanic acid or cephalosporins, is recommended for recurrent and chronic cases. Surgery, specifically adenoidectomy, is not the first-line treatment but is reserved for patients with chronic persistent adenoiditis and adenoid hypertrophy. Adenoidectomy has been shown to be effective regardless of the size of the adenoids. Primary prevention strategies for adenoiditis include maintaining good hygiene practices. Secondary prevention involves the use of antibiotics to prevent recurrence, particularly in cases with a history of rheumatic fever, to prevent pharyngitis caused by group A β-hemolytic streptococci.
